papers.title: Long-term safety profile of opicapone in patients with Parkinson's disease and early fluctuations.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Motor fluctuations frequently emerge within the first few years of levodopa treatment in Parkinson's disease (PD), increasing symptom burden and treatment complexity. While opicapone is an established adjunct therapy for motor fluctuations, its safety profile when initiated early in the course of fluctuating disease remains incompletely characterized. METHODS: This pooled post-hoc RESULTS: A total of 269 patients with recent motor fluctuations were included, of whom 228 entered open-label treatment. During the double-blind phase, TEAEs were reported in 55.9% of patients receiving opicapone and 50.9% receiving placebo, with no statistically significant difference between groups. Adverse events were mainly mild to moderate and occurred predominantly within the first 2-3 weeks declining thereafter. Dyskinesia was the most frequent TEAE (10.2% vs. 3.6%, p CONCLUSION: Opicapone demonstrated a favorable and consistent safety profile in patients with recent onset of motor fluctuations, with adverse events predominantly transient and manageable. Earlier initiation was not associated with an increased safety burden and showed numerically lower rates of overall TEAEs and dyskinesia compared with broader trial populations. These findings support the hypothesis that early optimization of levodopa therapy with opicapone does not accelerate the development of motor complications, supporting early COMT-inhibition in fluctuating PD.

papers.title: New insights of oligodendrocytes in the etiology of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Oligodendrocytes (OLs) are myelin-forming cells in the central nervous system (CNS), providing nutritional and metabolic support to axons. They also interact with other glial cells to regulate the microenvironment of the CNS. Recent clinical studies have revealed that OL dysfunction and white matter changes occur at an early stage of Parkinson's disease (PD) and may be associated with dopaminergic neuronal damage, postural, and gait disorders. However, whether these changes are primary drivers or secondary consequences of neurodegeneration remains to be determined. Biochemical and genetic studies have provided evidence for OL dysfunction in PD pathology. Mechanistic studies have shown that OL damage can disrupt neuronal integrity through communicating with neurons, and the aggregation of α-synuclein (α-Syn) in OLs also accelerates dopaminergic neuronal death. Emerging evidence suggests that OLs may play a significant role in the pathogenesis and progression of PD through their involvement in mitochondrial damage, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. In this review, we summarized current understanding of oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), OLs, myelination, and white matter in the pathogenesis of PD and discussed the potential therapy by targeting OLs for PD.

papers.title: The Glymphatic System in Traumatic Brain Injury, Subarachnoid Hemorrhage, and Neurodegeneration: A Unifying Neurobiological Framework.
papers.abstract: Whether glymphatic dysfunction drives or merely follows brain injury and neurodegeneration remains unresolved. The glymphatic system mediates the transport, exchange, and clearance of solutes between cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and interstitial fluid (ISF) through paravascular CSF influx, polarized aquaporin-4 (AQP4) at astrocytic endfeet, and meningeal lymphatic drainage. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on glymphatic regulation and its role in traumatic brain injury (TBI), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and neurodegeneration, and appraises imaging, biomarker, and therapeutic approaches. PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar were searched from inception to August 2026, and 128 sources were analyzed. In TBI, mechanical shear and NLR family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3)-dependent inflammation may alter AQP4 distribution and impair tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) clearance; however, glymphatic failure has not been established as the causal mediator of later neurodegeneration, which is likely multifactorial. After SAH, blood and fibrin may obstruct perivascular pathways, and hemoglobin, heme, and iron toxicity may further disrupt CSF-ISF exchange; these changes are associated with delayed cerebral ischemia, cortical spreading depolarizations, and post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus. Impaired clearance of Aβ, phosphorylated tau, and α-synuclein may link glymphatic dysfunction to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, although causality is unproven. Current imaging tools, including diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS), and biomarkers do not yet provide a validated measure of glymphatic function. Sleep optimization is a low-risk strategy, and controlled lumbar drainage has the strongest clinical evidence among CSF-dynamics approaches. Translation requires appropriate animal models and prospective TBI/SAH studies combining serial DTI-ALPS with cognitive follow-up.

papers.title: Electrovestibulography biomarkers differentiate schizophrenia from healthy controls: implications for the dopamine hypothesis.
papers.journal: The world journal of biological psychiatry : the official journal of the World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Previous studies have demonstrated that Electrovestibulography (EVestG) biomarkers for Parkinson's Disease are sensitive to dopamine levels. Given the dopamine hypothesis of Schizophrenia (SCZ), we recorded EVestG signals from 45 individuals with SCZ and 36 healthy controls to evaluate whether EVestG can differentiate these populations. METHODS: Features derived from field potentials (FP) and firing pattern interval histograms (IH33)-the two primary EVestG outcomes-were extracted and used to classify the two groups. RESULTS: We achieved a 78% cross-validated accuracy using a Naïve Bayes classifier. This classification performance was achieved despite nearly all SCZ participants being on antipsychotic medications with most on high (n = 21) or partial (n = 4) dopamine D2 receptor affinity, which would be expected to attenuate the dopaminergic signal. The exploratory separation of SCZ the sub-groups on high (N = 15) and low affinity (N = 15) D2 medications was achieved for the FP feature (p = 0.027). CONCLUSIONS: Features derived from both static and dynamic segments of the EVestG signal were altered in SCZ; features from dynamic segments-which impose greater metabolic demand on the vestibular system-showed more pronounced group differences than those from static segments.

papers.title: NADPH Oxidase-Related Oxidative Stress in Parkinson's Disease-Associated Cognitive Impairment: An Evidence-Focused Review.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment is a major non-motor manifestation of Parkinson's disease (PD); however, evidence linking specific NADPH oxidase (NOX) isoforms to cognition-related outcomes remains incompletely integrated. In this evidence-focused narrative review, a structured four-database search identified 12 studies for study-level synthesis: 10 rodent studies involving cognitive assessment in PD-relevant models and 2 contextual studies. The 10 core studies were appraised according to the directness with which NOX involvement was examined in relation to cognitive outcomes. The most direct experimental support centered on hippocampal NOX4- and NOX2/gp91phox-associated microglial signaling. Dentate-gyrus-targeted NOX4 knockdown attenuated learning and memory deficits, with concurrent reductions in proteinopathy-related changes. CD68-driven gp91phox knockdown similarly attenuated these deficits alongside reductions in inflammatory responses and neuronal and synaptic injury. Apocynin was classified as a NOX-targeted pharmacological intervention and improved learning and memory performance. However, its lack of target and isoform specificity precluded definitive attribution of the behavioral effect to NOX inhibition. Other studies contributed partial or supportive evidence, while complementary pathway-level evidence linked cognition-related inflammatory signaling to NOX1/NOX2 dependence. Human postmortem and canine biomarker studies have provided clinicopathological and comparative peripheral biomarker context, respectively, but they have not established a NOX-cognition relationship in human PD. Overall, the evidence suggests that NOX-related oxidative stress contributes to the development of learning and memory deficits in PD-relevant models. Because the principal NOX4 and gp91phox genetic interventions preceded model induction, the observed effects are best interpreted as protection during deficit development rather than reversal of established cognitive impairment. papers.title: Using High-Performance Liquid Chromatography to Study Alterations in Biogenic Amines in Drosophila Models of Brain Disorders.
papers.abstract: Many neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders are characterized by disruptions in brain neurotransmitters, including alterations in the levels of the biogenic amines (BAs) dopamine (DA) and serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT), as well as in their release or reuptake. These neurochemical changes correlate with distinct key behavioral phenotypes, such as locomotor deficits, sleep fragmentation, and altered stress responses, among others. Because the principal BA systems interact, disease models frequently show coordinated shifts across multiple amines rather than isolated changes in a single neurotransmitter. Therefore, accurate, simultaneous quantification of several BAs is essential for interpreting behavioral and genetic findings. Drosophila melanogaster offers a genetically tractable system for modeling such disorders and neurotransmitter changes, but BAs occur in fly brain tissue at very low, nanomolar-to-femtomolar concentrations, and the small size of the Drosophila central nervous system makes their detection technically challenging. This study describes a protocol to detect and quantify DA, 5-HT, and octopamine in fly brains using high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with electrochemical detection (HPLC-ECD). HPLC-ECD was applied to detect changes in brain DA and 5-HT in a fly model of Parkinson's disease based on dopaminergic overexpression of human alpha-synuclein. Applying this protocol to the alpha-synuclein Parkinson's disease model reveals significantly elevated dopamine, but unchanged serotonin, relative to controls, consistent with early compensatory dopaminergic mechanisms. This approach provides a sensitive, low-cost, and readily accessible method for multiplexed BA quantification from limited Drosophila tissue. It also enables systematic screening of genetic modifiers and candidate therapeutics targeting monoaminergic pathways relevant to human brain disorders.

papers.title: Neuromelanin-Sensitive MRI as a Marker of Clinical Severity and Disease Burden in Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: The neuropathology of Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized in part by the degeneration of catecholaminergic neurons, particularly dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC), yet no validated in vivo biomarker quantifies this process. Neuromelanin-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging (NM-MRI) enables noninvasive assessment of these neuronal populations, although relationships with clinical severity, disease burden, and progression remain incompletely defined. We conducted the first Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-guided systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis examining associations between NM-MRI measures and clinical outcomes in PD, including subgroup, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses. Reduced NM-MRI measures were associated with greater motor impairment (18 studies; pooled r = -0.406), longer disease duration (14; r = -0.426), higher Hoehn and Yahr stage (10; r = -0.336), and higher levodopa equivalent daily dose (6; r = -0.337) (all P < 0.001). Thirty-nine studies (1983 patients with PD) were included in the systematic review. Narrative synthesis demonstrated distinct SNpc/LC associations: SNpc measures were primarily associated with motor dysfunction and disease stage, displaying hemispheric asymmetry, intranigral topography, and phenotype-specific patterns, whereas LC measures were preferentially linked to cognitive, affective, autonomic, and sleep-related symptoms. Four longitudinal studies (~1.5-3 years) reported declines in selected NM-MRI measures (~5%-19% annually). Multimodal studies suggested NM-MRI captures a complementary dimension of nigrostriatal pathology alongside dopaminergic, iron-sensitive, and diffusion-based markers. NM-MRI provides a biologically interpretable in vivo measure of catecholaminergic neuron integrity and surviva

papers.title: Longitudinal Real-Time Quaking-Induced Conversion Analysis of Misfolded α-Synuclein in Idiopathic Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder Patients with Baseline Cerebrospinal Fluid Negativity.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: While most patients with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder (IRBD) show CSF misfolded α-synucleinpositivity, a subset tests negative with an uncertain underlying substrate that may include non-synucleinopathy conditions. OBJECTIVE AND METHODS: We performed a longitudinal study in polysomnography-confirmed IRBD patients with negative CSF α-synuclein at baseline (LP1) who underwent a second lumbar puncture (LP2). α-synuclein presence was determined by seed amplification assay. RESULTS: Among 43 αSyn -negative patients at LP1, 9 (20.9%) converted to αSyn positivity over a mean follow-up of 2.8 ± 2.3 years. At LP1, converters exhibited a higher burden of Parkinson's disease biomarkers, including hyposmia, abnormal dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography (DAT-SPECT), and increased REM sleep electromyographic activity, compared with patients with persistent αSyn negativity. Longer intervals between LP1 and LP2 were associated with higher αSyn shifting to positivity. CONCLUSION: Serial CSF αSyn assessments may identify a very early synucleinopathy stage. This strategy may improve patient selection for disease-modifying trials targeting αSyn. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Mediating Role of Emotional States Linking Parkinson's Disease Severity and Cognitive Function: A Cross-Instrument Comparison Using Two Cognitive Assessment Tools.
papers.journal: Journal of geriatric psychiatry and neurology
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThis cross-sectional study aimed to explore the relationships between disease severity and cognitive function in Parkinson's disease (PD), statistical indirect associations via anxiety and depression, and their stability across cognitive measures.MethodsA total of 255 PD patients were recruited. Disease severity was assessed using the Hoehn-Yahr (H-Y) stage. Cognitive function was evaluated with the Chinese Mini-Mental Status (CMMS) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Anxiety and depressive symptoms were measured using the Hamilton scales (HAMA/HAMD). Spearman's rank correlation and partial correlation analyses were used. papers.title: Predictors and prescribing patterns of definite anticholinergic medication use among community-dwelling older adults in Saudi Arabia: a retrospective multicenter cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Anticholinergic medications are associated with cognitive impairment and falls in older adults, yet multicenter evidence from Saudi Arabia remains limited. This study characterized prescribing patterns and factors associated with definite anticholinergic burden among older adults receiving outpatient care. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter cross-sectional study used outpatient records and dispensing data from two tertiary hospitals located in Al Khobar and Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia, between 2019 and 2024. Adults aged 60 years or older receiving at least one medication scoring 2 or 3 on the Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden (ACB) scale were included. Robust linear, negative binomial, and logistic regression models examined definite ACB score, additional qualifying medications, and multiple medication use. RESULTS: The study included 1,664 older adults with 2016 patient-medication instances. Polypharmacy was present in 84.3%, and 17.5% received multiple qualifying medications. Bladder antimuscarinics, antipsychotics, and tricyclic antidepressants accounted for 78.1% of medication instances, while urology, psychiatry, and neurology accounted for 72.0%. A corresponding coded diagnosis was identified for 20.0% of evaluable instances. Polypharmacy, hypertension, depression, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder were independently associated with all three outcomes. Schizophrenia showed the strongest associations with definite ACB score (B CONCLUSIONS: Definite anticholinergic use was concentrated within a limited number of medication classes and prescribing specialties. Psychiatric disorders and polypharmacy were consistently associated with higher burden, supporting targeted medication review in these patients and specialties.

papers.title: Ekbom Spectrum Psychosis Associated with 24-hour Continuous Subcutaneous Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa Infusion in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.journal: Clinical psychopharmacology and neuroscience : the official scientific journal of the Korean College of Neuropsychopharmacology
papers.abstract: Continuous subcutaneous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa infusion (CSFLI) is an emerging treatment for advanced Parkinson's disease (PD). We report atypical psychosis with Ekbom-like somatic hallucinations during CSFLI. A 74-year-old man with a 16-year history of PD (Hoehn and Yahr stage 3), mild cognitive impairment (Montreal Cognitive Assessment 25/30), and previous mild dopamine agonist-induced visual hallucinations received CSFLI for disabling motor fluctuations, dyskinesias, nocturnal rigidity, and severe morning akinesia inadequately controlled by oral therapy. Initial treatment was well tolerated, reducing OFF time, dyskinesias, and sleep disturbance. Because of recurrent motor fluctuations and nocturnal akinesia, infusion parameters were progressively increased to a daytime base rate of 0.48 ml/h and a nocturnal low-rate of 0.38 ml/h, corresponding to an estimated levodopa equivalent daily dose of approximately 1,868 mg/day. Seventy-two hours after ciprofloxacin initiation for an infected subcutaneous nodule, the patient developed vivid visual hallucinations that evolved into Ekbom-like somatic hallucinations, described as worms moving beneath the skin, leading to superficial self-inflicted lacerations. Orientation remained preserved and no delirium features were observed. Initial reduction of infusion parameters, safinamide discontinuation, and quetiapine produced only partial benefit. A subsequent selective reduction of the nocturnal low-rate from 0.36 to 0.30 ml/h was associated with a clinically meaningful reduction in psychotic symptoms, although residual hallucinations and worsening morning akinesia persisted. This case suggests that psychosis during CSFLI may reflect the interaction between neuropsychiatric vulnerability, ciprofloxacin exposure, and sustained nocturnal dopaminergic stimulation. Although causality cannot be inferred, careful nocturnal titration may help clinicians recognize and manage atypical psychotic manifestations early in susceptible pati

papers.title: Effects of exercise on balance in people with Parkinson's disease: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postural instability and impaired balance are disabling, levodopa-resistant features of Parkinson's disease (PD) and leading contributors to falls. Many systematic reviews and meta-analyses (SR/MAs) report that exercise improves balance, but they differ in modality, comparator, instrument and rigor and have not been synthesized and graded as a whole. We conducted an umbrella review of meta-analytic evidence on exercise and balance in PD. METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 and umbrella-review methodology, PubMed and Web of Science were searched from inception to 8 June 2026. Pairwise SR/MAs of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reporting balance performance (Berg Balance Scale [BBS], Mini-BESTest), mobility (Timed Up-and-Go [TUG]) or falls in PD were eligible; network meta-analyses were supporting evidence only. We extracted the pooled random-effects estimates as reported by each review (no re-pooling of individual-trial data), harmonized their direction, and interpreted standardized effects as small/moderate/large. Methodological quality, primary-study overlap and certainty were appraised with AMSTAR-2, the corrected covered area (CCA) and GRADE. RESULTS: From 161 unique records, 20 pairwise meta-analyses were included, spanning aerobic, resistance, aquatic, dance, VR/exergaming, traditional Chinese exercise, and home-based and group formats. Exercise improved balance in most modalities, though not universally (resistance training and one mixed-exercise review were non-significant). Because estimates came from separate meta-analyses, they are not directly comparable; standardized balance-performance effects ranged from small (g = 0.33, 95% CI 0.11-0.55) to large (aerobic, BBS g = 0.99, 0.76-1.23). Evidence on falls was inconsistent (proportion of fallers unchanged; fall rate reduced). Between-review overlap was very high at the BBS node (CCA = 16.8%). papers.title: MUSIC-PD: A Delphi-Derived, Culturally Adaptable Music Therapy Protocol for Parkinson's Disease Rehabilitation.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Music-based interventions have shown promise in Parkinson's disease (PD) rehabilitation. However, variability in intervention design, delivery, dose, and documentation limits clinical translation. OBJECTIVE: The aim of the study was to develop a consensus-based music therapy protocol for PD, designed to permit cultural and linguistic adaptation. METHODS: A PRISMA-informed evidence-mapping review identified music-based and rhythm-based interventions relevant to PD rehabilitation. Findings informed a modified Delphi process involving a multidisciplinary expert panel of movement disorder neurologists, qualified music therapists, and people with PD. Round 1 generated qualitative inputs on therapeutic domains, safety, feasibility, and cultural adaptation. These were synthesized into 36 structured statements and rated in Round 2 using a 5-point Likert scale. Consensus was predefined as ≥80% agreement. RESULTS: The evidence map included 32 studies and identified 3 therapeutic clusters: motor/gait rehabilitation, voice-respiratory communication, and nonmotor cognitive-affective engagement. Of the 36 Delphi statements, 33 reached consensus. High-convergence domains included patient-preferred familiar music, cultural adaptation, rhythmic auditory stimulation for gait rehabilitation, multidomain symptom targeting, and vocal rehabilitation. The final framework was organized into LAYA-Locomotor Auditory Yielding Activation Module, NADA-Neurocognitive and Affective Domain Activation Module, and RAGA-Respiratory Aerodynamic Glottal Activation Module. The protocol incorporated session-selection rules, safety screening, difficulty levels, active and/or receptive therapy components, flexible pragmatic session guidance, caregiver-supported practice, and a proposed session-planning/documentation resource. CONCLUSION: MUSIC-PD provides a structured, Delphi-derived, and panel-approved framework for integrating music-based interventions into multidisciplinary PD rehabil

papers.title: Effects of dance for Parkinson's disease on habitual physical activity: a quasi-experimental controlled study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite symptomatic therapies for PD, habitual physical activity inevitably declines as the disease progresses, leading to increased sedentary behavior. While dance programs have demonstrated a multitude of benefits including motor, non-motor, and psychological aspects, it has not yet been objectively determined if dance can improve habitual physical activity in people living with PD. AIM: This study explored whether participation in Dance for Parkinson's Disease classes was associated with changes in habitual physical activity in people with PD. DESIGN: A quasi-experimental controlled efficacy study, with pre and post-testing of two parallel groups (dance versus control). POPULATION: Thirty-three participants with PD allocated to a dance group (DG; n METHODS: The DG undertook a one-hour Dance for Parkinson's Disease (DfPD®) -based class, twice weekly for 12 weeks (intervention). The CG had treatment as usual. ActivPAL™ accelerometers monitored habitual physical activity for five consecutive days pre-and post-intervention. Sit/lie duration (min), standing duration (min), stepping duration (min), sit/stand movements (count), stand/sit movements (count), daily step count, and energy expenditure (MET-h/day) were measured. RESULTS: No significant between-group differences were observed for any ActivPAL outcome. However, increases in daily stepping duration and step count demonstrated moderate-to-large effect sizes (d CONCLUSION: Participation in a dance for Parkinson's disease program did not significantly alter pre- to post-program habitual physical activity. Larger adequately powered trials are required to determine whether participation in dance programs can influence habitual physical activity in people with Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: Early health technology assessment of machine learning-enabled remote monitoring for advanced Parkinson disease.
papers.journal: International journal of technology assessment in health care
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Advanced Parkinson disease (APD) is often under-recognized, which may delay treatment optimization and referral for device-aided therapy assessment. Machine learning-enabled remote monitoring systems (ML-RMS) may support earlier recognition of progression, but their value depends on whether alerts lead to clinical action and patient benefit. METHODS: We developed a Markov model comparing standard care with ML-RMS-supported care from the Finnish health care perspective. The model simulated persons with Parkinson disease at risk of APD over 16 years. The base case assumed ML-RMS sensitivity and specificity of 88 percent and 62 percent. Costs, quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), incremental cost-effectiveness ratios, and incremental net monetary benefit were estimated. Scenario and probabilistic sensitivity analyses explored diagnostic accuracy, monitoring costs, direct quality-of-life effects, deep brain stimulation (DBS) costs, pathway timing, and delayed nursing home admission. RESULTS: In the base case, ML-RMS generated 0.0044 additional QALYs at an additional cost of €761 per patient, resulting in an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €172,023 per QALY gained. At a willingness-to-pay threshold of €35,000 per QALY, the incremental net monetary benefit was negative. Scenario analyses indicated that ML-RMS could become cost-effective if active monitoring produced direct quality-of-life gains or delayed nursing home admission. CONCLUSIONS: ML-RMS is unlikely to be economically favorable if limited to earlier APD recognition and timely DBS treatment in a small eligible subgroup. Its value depends on whether monitoring changes care pathways, improves patient outcomes, or reduces long-term care needs. Future studies should prioritize clinical utility, quality-of-life effects, treatment decisions, and institutional care.

papers.title: Is it truly patient-centered? Doctor-patient communication in remote programming for Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Patients with Parkinson's disease require frequent programming after deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery to maintain therapeutic efficacy. Although remote programming promises a more patient-centered and accessible healthcare model, the transition from in-person to virtual visits may introduce unique barriers that compromise this innovative care model. From a doctor-patient communication perspective, this study explores these specific communication barriers and their subsequent impact on programming outcomes and patient experience. METHODS: Non-participatory observation and in-depth interviews were used to understand the experiences of patients, caregivers, and doctors regarding communication during remote programming of DBS. Thematic analysis was applied to analyze the qualitative data. RESULTS: A total of 49 participants were enrolled. Three themes were identified: Structural changes in doctor-patient communication; Expanded patient responsibility; and Weakened emotional support. Findings indicate that Parkinson's patients face new barriers to communication access, heavier burdens of self-expression, and poorer outcomes in emotional communication. CONCLUSION: The shift in programming models has introduced numerous new challenges for patients and their caregivers, including mastering digital devices, ensuring that home environments are suitable for online consultations, accurately describing symptoms, and accepting the absence of emotional comfort.

papers.title: Spectral-spatial Modeling of Neural Couplings in Functional Connectivity of Motor Networks.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Functional neural connectivity reflects coordinated interactions within brain networks in both health and disease. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) is widely used for this purpose, but its pairwise formulations overlook spatially distributed, spectrally correlated structures in neural activity that arises from complex brain circuits. NEW METHOD: We developed a spectral-spatial generalized linear model (SS-GLM) to characterize the high-frequency response as the integrated outcome of multiple low-frequency phase sources across channels and frequencies. Our method also utilizes a regularization strategy to mitigate predictor collinearity and spurious effects for stable attribution of network-level coupling estimates. RESULTS: Validation was performed using both synthetic data and human motor network recordings from 25 patients with Parkinson's disease undergoing deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery. In synthetic analyses, SS-GLM accurately recovered ground-truth coupling configurations under multiple plausible scenarios. In real data, the framework revealed coherent cortico-subthalamic coupling patterns across distinct motor tasks that aligned with clinically effective DBS contacts and their anatomical organization. COMPARISON WITH EXISTING METHODS: Conventional pairwise PAC metrics, such as the modulation index and GLM assess interactions in isolation. In contrast, SS-GLM jointly models distributed predictors and yields spatially localized, spectrally specific coupling estimates that also achieve stronger correspondence with clinical stimulation outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: This work offers a principled and extensible framework for advancing functional connectivity analyses, with improved interpretability of network-level interactions, enhanced robustness to confounds, and broad potential for future applications in systems neuroscience and neuro-engineering research.

papers.title: Deep learning models to detect neurodegenerative diseases across different modalities, datasets, and stages: A systematic review.
papers.journal: Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine
papers.abstract: BackgroundNeurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's pose significant diagnostic challenges because they are incurable. Their symptoms often overlap with those of normal ageing and involve progressive neuronal loss. This makes early prediction, proper diagnosis, and ongoing monitoring crucial at every stage of the disease. Deep learning has become a useful tool for handling different types of data. However, the performance of these models relies heavily on the availability and variety of data, making it important to characterize datasets.ObjectiveThis PRISMA-based systematic review looks at 111 studies from 2019 to April 2026, organized into three clinical stages of neurodegenerative diseases: early prediction, diagnosis, and progression.MethodsEach study is assessed across four dimensions: data type (neuroimaging or non-neuroimaging), datasets (open-access, self-created, or hybrid), deep learning model architecture, and the use of explainable AI.ResultsMRI is the only imaging modality that spans all three stages. Speech is the most common non-neuroimaging method for diagnosis, while gait is used only for diagnosis and progression. The ADNI and PPMI datasets are the most commonly used. Self-created datasets introduce new modalities such as ECG and iPSCs, which are not found in open-access datasets. CNNs are the leading models for neuroimaging tasks, while LSTMs and RNNs capture temporal patterns in longitudinal datasets. Survival models are exclusively used for ALS and LATE. Fewer than 6% of the studies used confirmed XAI. Only 2 of the 111 studies validated their results on an independent external cohort.ConclusionThis review is the only one that covers all three disease stages across multiple neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Genetic Analysis of the SLC38A6 Gene in Chinese Patients with Essential Tremor: Not Causative, But Rather an Additional Susceptibility Gene?
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: A recent study implicated rare SLC38A6 variants in Han Chinese cases of essential tremor (ET). OBJECTIVES: To validate the association between SLC38A6 and ET in an independent cohort via gene-level burden analysis and family co-segregation. METHODS: We sequenced all coding exons and splice sites of SLC38A6 in 724 Han Chinese ET patients and 606 controls, performing gene-level burden tests and co-segregation analysis. RESULTS: Eleven rare variants were identified. The most recurrent variant, c.323A>T (p.Y108F), was enriched in cases (3.45% vs. 1.16%; odds ratio [OR] 3.06, 95% confidence interval [95% CI] 1.31-7.13, P = 0.0065). Gene-level analysis showed significantly more rare-variant carriers in cases than in controls (7.73% vs. 3.63%; OR 2.23, 95% CI 1.34-3.69, P = 0.0015), confirmed by sequence kernel association test (SKAT) (P = 0.0257). Six of 12 families showed co-segregation of c.323A>T (p.Y108F), c.719C>A (p.P240Q), or c.752A>G (p.Y251C) with ET. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support SLC38A6 as a candidate susceptibility gene for ET in Han Chinese. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Clinical and genetic characteristics of patients with early-onset or familial parkinsonism: A retrospective single-center cohort.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer's disease. Hereditary causes account for 10-15% of cases but present considerably more complex clinical manifestations than idiopathic cases. It is therefore imperative to enhance clinicians' recognition of hereditary forms. METHODS: This study enrolled 29 patients with early‑onset or familial parkinsonism. 17 cases were identified with reportable genetic findings using PD-targeted or movement disorders gene panels. Clinical data and genetic data were collected. RESULTS: Among 17 patients, PARK2/PRKN (n = 9) and PARK8/LRRK2 (n = 5) were predominant subtypes, with two cases of PARK14/PLA2G6, and one case of PARK18/EIF4G1. Clinically, bradykinesia affected 17/17 patients, rigidity 15/17, tremor 13/17, and dystonia 7/17 (including one oculogyric crisis). Hyperreflexia occurred in 6/17, cognitive impairment in 2/17, pyramidal signs in 2/17, ataxic dysarthria 1/17, and pes cavus in 1/17. Diurnal fluctuation and sleep benefit occurred exclusively in PARK2/PRKN and PARK14/PLA2G6 patients. Among patients with PRKN, 7/9 exhibited diurnal fluctuations: five had exon rearrangements, one had a splicing mutation, and one had a homozygous variant. Conversely, the two PARK2/PRKN patients without diurnal fluctuations showed no exon deletions/duplications. PARK18/EIF4G1 mutations may manifest incomplete penetrance. CONCLUSION: Among PARK2/PRKN patients in our cohort, a potential association between diurnal fluctuation and exon rearrangements may exist, although this observation requires cautious interpretation. Furthermore, these variants appear to cluster within the N-terminal region of the protein (the start of the RING1 domain and preceding regions). Beyond the common PARK2/PRKN subtype, PARK14/PLA2G6 may also be linked to diurnal fluctuation and sleep benefit.
